quests.scene: Your roommate is playing music while you study. You have an exam tomorrow morning and you're on good terms with her.
options: Your music is way too loud, you know.
I'm trying to study here, is that too much to ask? Some of us actually have exams.
Could you turn it down a bit? I've got an exam tomorrow.
Do you have to play music right now?
quests.hint: Give the reason; it makes the request easy to grant.
quests.explanation: A polite request with a reason keeps things friendly and makes it easy for her to agree. Complaints or rhetorical questions sound like accusations.
quests.culturalNote: Between roommates, a reason plus a soft request usually works better than criticism.

quests.scene: You need to miss next Friday's shift because of a dentist appointment. You're asking a coworker to cover it.
options: I need Friday off, so I've put you down for my shift.
Friday doesn't work for me at all, so could you please sort something out before the rota goes up next week?
Can anyone take my Friday shift? I really don't mind who it is.
Would you be able to swap Friday's shift with me? I've got a dentist appointment.
quests.hint: Ask a person directly, don't assume or broadcast.
quests.explanation: Asking one person directly, with a reason, respects her choice. Assuming she'll cover or asking vaguely leaves her unsure or pressured.
quests.culturalNote: Shift swaps rely on goodwill, so asking rather than telling matters.

quests.scene: You're going away for a week and want your neighbor to take in your parcels while you're gone.
options: If a parcel comes, just take it, okay?
Could you look after my place next week while I'm away? I'll owe you one, promise.
I'm away next week — would you mind taking in any parcels for me?
Could you keep an eye on things for me?
quests.hint: Be specific about exactly what you're asking.
quests.explanation: A specific request lets your neighbor decide easily. Vague or open-ended requests leave him unsure what's expected.
quests.culturalNote: Specific requests are easier to accept because the size of the favor is clear.

quests.scene: Your friend is moving flats on Saturday and mentions she has too many boxes. You'd like to help and have a car.
options: Do you need a hand on Saturday? I can bring my car.
Moving is such a pain, I don't envy you.
Let me know if you need anything sometime.
I'm free Saturday if nobody else can help.
quests.hint: An offer works best when it names what you can actually do.
quests.explanation: A concrete offer with a specific day and resource is easy to accept. Sympathy or open-ended offers rarely turn into help.
quests.culturalNote: Vague offers like 'let me know' often go unused because they put the effort on the other person.

quests.scene: Your manager says, 'I can extend the deadline if you need it.' You do need two more days to check the figures.
options: Yes, that would help — two more days would let me check the figures properly.
No, I'll manage, don't worry about it.
If you think it's best, that's fine with me. I'm happy to go with whatever you decide is easiest.
Sure, but I probably won't need all of it.
quests.hint: When you genuinely need something, say so and say how much.
quests.explanation: Accepting with a clear reason and amount shows you're planning carefully. Refusing or being noncommittal risks either rushing or confusion.
quests.culturalNote: Managers usually prefer specific requests to vague acceptance.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: A coworker offers you a lift home, but you prefer to walk after a long day at your desk.
options: No thanks, I don't really like getting into other people's cars, it makes me a bit anxious.
It's fine, I'd rather walk. Don't offer again.
Thanks so much, but I'm okay.
Thanks, but I like the walk after a long day — see you tomorrow!
quests.hint: Decline in a way that keeps the offer feeling welcome.
quests.explanation: Thanking her and giving a light reason keeps the door open. Cold or absolute refusals make the offer feel unwelcome.
quests.culturalNote: A reason that's about you, not them, avoids implying criticism.

quests.scene: You're meeting a friend for lunch but a work meeting has just been scheduled at noon.
options: Lunch is off, work's crazy.
Can we do lunch another day instead? I'm not sure when I'll be free, but I'll let you know.
My boss made me stay, so I can't come.
I'm so sorry, a meeting came up at noon. Can we move lunch to Thursday?
quests.hint: Offer a specific alternative, not just a cancellation.
quests.explanation: Apologizing and proposing a concrete new time shows you value the plan. Vague postponement leaves your friend waiting.
quests.culturalNote: Cancelling with a new time proposed reassures the other person it's not a brush-off.

quests.scene: You're phoning to cancel your Thursday dentist appointment and would like to rebook.
options: I won't be coming Thursday.
Can you cancel my appointment on Thursday please? Something's come up and I can't say when I'll be free.
I need to cancel my Thursday appointment. Could I rebook for next week?
I might not make Thursday, I'll let you know.
quests.hint: A cancellation call should include the next step you want.
quests.explanation: Stating the cancellation and the rebooking request helps the receptionist help you. Vague cancellations leave them unsure.
quests.culturalNote: Clinics value early cancellation with a rebooking request.

quests.scene: A friend asks the group where to eat. You're vegetarian but flexible about cuisine.
options: I'm happy with anything, as long as there's a vegetarian option.
I don't mind, you decide.
Not Italian again — I always end up with just plain pasta and everyone else gets the good dishes.
Anywhere is fine. I'll just eat a salad.
quests.hint: Share the one constraint that matters and stay flexible otherwise.
quests.explanation: Naming your one need while staying open helps the group choose well. Full deference or complaints don't help them pick.
quests.culturalNote: Stating dietary needs early avoids awkward situations at the restaurant.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: A ticket inspector on a bus asks for your ticket, but your wallet is at home and you didn't buy one on the app.
options: I always have a ticket, so I really don't know what happened here, it must have been the app playing up again.
The machine wasn't working when I got on.
It's not my fault, I just forgot my wallet.
I'm sorry, I left my wallet at home. Is there a way I can pay you now or give my details?
quests.hint: Be honest and offer a solution.
quests.explanation: Admitting the mistake and offering to fix it shows good faith. Excuses or invented stories can make things worse.
quests.culturalNote: Inspectors deal with excuses constantly; honesty tends to get a better reception.

quests.scene: The waiter brings a fish dish, but you ordered chicken and you don't eat fish.
options: This isn't what I ordered. Take it back.
Did you mix up the tables? This looks wrong.
I'll just eat it, it's fine.
Excuse me, I think this is fish — I ordered the chicken.
quests.hint: State the problem simply, without blame.
quests.explanation: Naming the mismatch and what you ordered lets him fix it quickly. Blame or silence leaves you with a meal you can't eat.
quests.culturalNote: Restaurants expect order mistakes and respond well to calm, specific corrections.

quests.scene: The airline agent says your flight will be delayed two hours. You have a connecting flight to Lisbon.
options: This is ridiculous, I'm going to miss everything.
Could you tell me whether I'll still make my connection to Lisbon?
How long will it be delayed? Two hours is far too long and nobody has told us anything useful yet.
Please just get me on another flight.
quests.hint: Ask about the specific consequence you care about.
quests.explanation: A specific question about your connection points the agent toward a solution. Complaints or demands don't give her a clear task.
quests.culturalNote: Agents can only fix what they hear; specific questions get better answers than general frustration.

quests.scene: In a group project, a teammate suggests you take the slides. You'd rather do the data analysis, which you've done more of.
options: I don't want the slides, so please give them to someone else, because I hate designing that stuff.
That works, but could I take the data section instead? I've done more of that.
Fine, whatever you want.
I'd do it differently, but go ahead.
quests.hint: Counter-propose with a reason that helps the group.
quests.explanation: Suggesting an alternative with a reason keeps the plan collaborative. Refusing or giving in silently risks resentment.
quests.culturalNote: Group work runs smoother when preferences are stated openly.

quests.scene: Your housemate suggests a cleaning rota. You think the bathroom should alternate weekly.
options: Sounds fair — could we alternate weeks for the bathroom?
I'll clean when I have time.
I already do most of it.
Whatever, just tell me what to do and I'll do it, I don't really have any strong opinion.
quests.hint: Agree in principle and suggest a fair tweak.
quests.explanation: Agreeing while proposing a specific change keeps it cooperative. Vague or defensive replies don't settle anything.
quests.culturalNote: Shared living works best when tasks are clearly divided.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: A coworker asks if you can cover reception for ten minutes. You're in the middle of finishing a report.
options: I'm busy, ask someone else.
Sure, I'll drop everything right now and cover reception for as long as you need me to.
Why can't you ask Tom?
I'm in the middle of something — can I come in fifteen minutes?
quests.hint: You can be helpful and honest about timing.
quests.explanation: Offering a later time is honest and still helpful. Refusing outright or deflecting is cold; dropping everything creates its own problems.
quests.culturalNote: Colleagues usually prefer a realistic time to an outright no.

quests.scene: A friend asks to borrow your new car for the weekend. You're nervous about lending it out.
options: Sorry, my insurance doesn't cover other drivers, and the company would be furious if anything happened to it.
I don't lend my car to anyone.
I'd rather keep the car this weekend — it's still new and I'm nervous about it. Sorry!
Maybe. Ask me again on Friday.
quests.hint: An honest reason is better than an invented excuse.
quests.explanation: Honesty about your own worry protects the friendship. Invented reasons or vague answers may cause trouble later.
quests.culturalNote: Personal reasons are usually accepted more than invented rules.

quests.scene: A classmate asks to copy your homework before class because he didn't finish.
options: I can't let you copy it, but I can go through the tricky parts with you.
No way, that's cheating.
Sure, but don't tell the teacher I let you, and don't copy every single answer word for word.
Ask someone else.
quests.hint: Refuse the request but stay helpful.
quests.explanation: Declining while offering real help keeps the relationship intact and stays honest. Flat refusals or agreeing to cheat both cost you.
quests.culturalNote: Boundaries stay friendlier when paired with another way to help.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: Your elderly neighbor asks you to change a lightbulb. You're already late for work.
options: I'm late for work, sorry.
I'll do it this weekend, I promise.
Can't you get someone else to do it? There must be somebody in the building who's free right now.
I'm running late this morning, but I can do it tonight around seven — okay?
quests.hint: Say when you can help.
quests.explanation: Offering a specific time shows you care. Vague promises or deflection leave her waiting.
quests.culturalNote: Older neighbors often value a firm time to a vague promise.

quests.scene: A colleague stayed late to help you finish a presentation. You want to thank her.
options: Thanks, I owe you.
Thanks for staying — I couldn't have finished the slides without you.
Thanks, though I would have managed to finish it on my own without any trouble.
You didn't have to stay so long.
quests.hint: Thank her for the specific thing she did.
quests.explanation: Specific thanks makes her feel her effort mattered. Casual or minimizing thanks lessens it.
quests.culturalNote: Naming what someone did makes thanks more meaningful.

quests.scene: A teacher stayed after class to explain a topic you didn't understand. You finally get it.
options: Thanks, that was fine.
Thank you for staying — I finally understand it.
Thanks. I still don't get some of it though.
Okay, I understand now, bye.
quests.hint: Say what her time achieved.
quests.explanation: Naming the result tells her the effort worked. Bare thanks or hurried exits miss the moment.
quests.culturalNote: Teachers appreciate hearing that their time helped.

quests.scene: Your boss says, 'Great job on the report.' Several colleagues contributed to it.
options: Oh, it was nothing.
I know, I worked really hard on it.
Thank you — the team helped a lot, especially Nina with the figures.
Thanks, but it could have been better if we'd had a little more time to work on it.
quests.hint: Accept praise and share credit where due.
quests.explanation: Thanking your boss and crediting others shows humility and fairness. Downplaying or self-promoting weakens the moment.
quests.culturalNote: Sharing credit in workplaces builds team trust.

quests.scene: You're sightseeing and want a photo of you and your friend. A stranger is standing nearby.
options: Excuse me, would you mind taking a photo of us?
Take our photo, will you?
Can you take a photo? It takes two seconds.
Do you know how to use a phone camera?
quests.hint: Ask politely and don't test their skills.
quests.explanation: A polite question makes the favor easy to grant. Commands or testing feel impolite.
quests.culturalNote: Tourists commonly ask strangers for photos; a polite opener is expected.

quests.scene: The train is crowded and someone's bag is on the only free seat.
options: Sorry, would you mind moving your bag so I can sit?
Move your bag. Other people need seats.
Excuse me, is that bag paying for a seat?
Could someone move their bag? People need seats.
quests.hint: Speak to the person directly and politely.
quests.explanation: A polite direct request gets action without causing offense. Sarcasm or general announcements create conflict.
quests.culturalNote: On public transport, a courteous direct request usually works.

quests.scene: You're in a hospital lobby for a blood test appointment and don't know where to go.
options: Where's the blood test place?
Excuse me, where should I go for my blood test appointment?
I have an appointment here today — could you tell me where I'm supposed to go for it?
Is this the right place?
quests.hint: Include the reason so staff can point you right.
quests.explanation: Naming your appointment type lets the receptionist direct you immediately. Vague questions slow things down.
quests.culturalNote: Hospital staff handle many visitors; specific information helps.

quests.scene: A new colleague keeps asking questions while you're trying to meet a deadline.
options: I'm busy. Read the manual.
Ask me later, I'm swamped.
Happy to help — can we go through it at three? I need to finish this first.
Sure, ask away, I'll do this report later, it's not really that urgent anyway, don't worry.
quests.hint: Be helpful while protecting your deadline.
quests.explanation: Proposing a specific time is generous and clear. Curt replies feel dismissive; dropping everything harms your work.
quests.culturalNote: Newcomers usually value being told when help is available.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: A friend keeps texting you late at night for advice on a personal problem. You're exhausted.
options: Stop texting me at night.
I want to help, but I'm off to bed — can we talk tomorrow morning?
I'll reply when I can.
Sure, let's talk it through right now, I can stay up as long as you need me to tonight.
quests.hint: Set a boundary and offer another time.
quests.explanation: Caring while stating your limit protects both of you. Blunt or absent replies feel like rejection.
quests.culturalNote: Friends usually understand boundaries when they're framed with care.

quests.scene: Your father asks for help with online banking. He's slow with apps and gets nervous.
options: Here, let me do it.
It's really simple, Dad, you just follow the instructions on the screen and press the green button.
Let's do it together step by step — you press the buttons and I'll guide you.
Ask the bank, they can explain it better.
quests.hint: Help in a way that builds his confidence.
quests.explanation: Guiding him keeps him in control and helps him learn. Doing it for him or dismissing his concern doesn't.
quests.culturalNote: Teaching older relatives new technology works best when they stay in control.

quests.scene: You'd like to take a specific Friday off for a family event and need to ask your manager.
options: I'm taking Friday the 14th off.
Would it be possible to take Friday the 14th off? I've got a family event.
Can I have some days off next month, whichever?
I've already booked flights for the 14th, so I'll be away that whole day and the weekend.
quests.hint: Ask for specific dates and give context.
quests.explanation: A specific request with a reason lets your manager decide. Announcing or vague asking leaves them uncomfortable.
quests.culturalNote: Requesting rather than announcing time off shows respect for the team.

quests.scene: The office kitchen sink has been full of dirty mugs for a week. You'd like to raise it without blaming anyone.
options: Who keeps leaving mugs in the sink?
Could we all try to rinse our mugs before leaving? The sink's been full lately.
Some people here clearly weren't taught to clean up after themselves, and it's getting tiresome.
I'll clean it, but it's the last time.
quests.hint: Address the group, not an individual.
quests.explanation: A group-wide, forward-looking request avoids blame. Accusations and passive-aggressive remarks cause resentment.
quests.culturalNote: Shared-space issues are best raised as group agreements.

quests.scene: You want a friend's honest feedback on your CV before sending it out today.
options: Could you look over my CV and tell me anything that seems unclear?
Tell me my CV is fine, please.
I've finished my CV, what do you think? I think it's pretty much perfect, to be honest.
Read this quickly, I need to send it.
quests.hint: Ask for what you genuinely need.
quests.explanation: Asking for specific feedback invites honest, useful comments. Asking for reassurance or rushing them doesn't.
quests.culturalNote: Specific feedback requests usually get better responses than general ones.
